kandidater.beskrivning: Neolithic polished stone axehead fragment. From towards the butt end, but both ends broken and large flake broken off one surface (ancient damage). Longitudinal striations on middle of both surfaces, and diagonal striations at the edges/sides - presumably from polishing. kategorier: Neolithic artefacts in the Portable Antiquities Scheme

kandidater.beskrivning: Igneous Stone, finder suggests an origin in Coniston area of the Lake District, citing his personal knowledge of geological topics. The stone is pale grey green in colour, dense and vesicular with crystalline and micaceous inclusions. A more local origin as a glacial erratic is possible. Possible Axe head. Stone of lentoid section, slightly tapered; a chip on one side has subsequently been smoothed, though whether by human or natural agency is uncertain. The vesicular nature of the material would not seem as apt to the making of a polished axe head as the more familiar Langdale tuff. Nor is this reporter aware of a trade in axe blanks comparable with that in polished axes. However, unpolished axes, maces and axe hammers are a feature of Early Bronze Age activity, and like the Neolithic versions may equally have been charged with significance beyond their primary functions - which are also debated. Suggested date: Possibly Neolithic to Early Bronze Age, 3500-1500 BC. Length: 127mm, Width: 67mm, Thickness: 35mm, Weight: circa 500gms.
kategorier: Bronze Age stone axes in the Portable Antiquities Scheme

kandidater.fil: File:Neolithic polished stone Langdale Tuff axehead. (FindID 917147).jpg
kandidater.upphovsperson: The Portable Antiquities Scheme, Lucy Bevan, 2018-10-03 16:19:10
kandidater.kredit: https://finds.org.uk/database/ajax/download/id/1029602 Catalog: https://finds.org.uk/database/images/image/id/1029602/recordtype/artefacts archive copy at the Wayback Machine Artefact: https://finds.org.uk/database/artefacts/record/id/917147
kandidater.beskrivning: An incomplete polished stone axehead, probably of Langdale Tuff. The handaxe has an assymetrical break at the butt end. The surface of the axe is granular but smooth with a distinct grey-green hue. The surfaces are finely polished with striations visible and very little visible of any flaking scars from the rough-out stage of manufacture. The object is sub-rectangular and tapers toward the butt and has a pointed oval section. The blade end tapers out to the side and in along the blade edge. The cutting edge is assymetical and has a large flake missing, probably post depositional damage as the stone revealed is darker. One face has a large flake missing at the distal end. The butt end is missing due to a crude break. Date: Neolithic Dimensions: 91.9mm x 64.6mm x 34.4mm. Weight: 273g. The object is a probable Langdale polished axehead. The Langdale tuff's in the Lake District are soft, volcanic deposits and polished axe-heads from this source are found throughout the country. This rock type is formed from compressed volcanic ash and has a fine grained composition with infrequent crystalline inclusions. Tuff is found in Britain and Ireland in a band that runs down the Irish Sea from the Lake District, County Antrim (Ireland), through North Wales and into Cornwall and Devon. Volcanic tuff is similar to flint in that it can be finely worked, ground and polished to form a variety of tools; however axes are the most common find type and were used across Northern Europe during the Neolithic period Sally Taylor MSc has an analysed the axe and has commented: Dorset Axe L 940mm W 670mm Th 370mm Wt 270g Blade section of a finely worked Langdale polished axe, broken in antiquity. Symmetrical edges in plan and a very even outline in profile; rounded oval in cross-section, with no triangular crest where the blade face rises to meet the body of the axe - further evidence of fine work. Minimal polished out flake scars - two small examples observed in the blade section. Thin side facets at the blade end reducing to very straight, slightly rounded edges separating the two faces of the axe; fine diagonal polishing striations evident along the edges of both sides. Clear signs of use - an obliquely worn blade with small chips along the edge. A large impact removal on one face, behind the worn side of the blade; repair of this damage by repolishing, evidenced by a smoothed dip in the face surface towards the blade edge and visible polishing striations. In what would have been the mid-section of the original axe (at the broken end of the section seen) a band of shallow fine pitting across both faces, not seen at the edges - evidence of hafting wear. Three break surfaces, two with hinge fractures; an additional modern break makes it difficult to determine the removal sequence and attribute intentionality.

kandidater.kredit: https://finds.org.uk/database/ajax/download/id/553352 Catalog: https://finds.org.uk/database/images/image/id/553352/recordtype/artefacts archive copy at the Wayback Machine Artefact: https://finds.org.uk/database/artefacts/record/id/767612
kandidater.beskrivning: A damaged and incomplete stone axe of Neolithic date, probably a Group VI Langdale axe. The stone axe has been polished and is grey-green in colour. The axe is made from a fine-grained siliceous tuff, a sedimentary volcanic rock which was orignally deposited in water and is likely to be from the Great Langdale quarries in Cumbria. The axe is damaged, missing most of one side and some of the blade edge on both surfaces. The break may have occured during use, as it appears to originate from the blade end (Alison Roberts pers. comm ). c. 4000-2351 BC.
